name: Bianca Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government, sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me what a normal day at the clinic appointments centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take calls from people who need to move an appointment because a bus is late, a child is ill or the letter went to the wrong address. I check the clinic diary, then I read the new time back slowly. Saturday shifts pay extra, and I've held them for years. I don't use AI tools; the last thing I want is another screen guessing what a worried caller meant.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills and decisions at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ellis, my partner, drives a town bus. Our son and daughter are grown and pay their own rent. The Saturday premium lifts my wages above the usual agent rate, and we have about nine months of expenses saved. We still pay a mortgage, so I like to know the money is there before I agree to anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other agents the clinic diary can already send reminders, and I don't mind that. Somebody still has to ask if the patient can actually get to a changed appointment. A little faster filing isn't a reason to put a machine between the caller and the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Saturday hours should remain and Ellis should still have his bus shifts. Nine months saved means we can replace a cooker without a crisis, though the mortgage is a monthly fact. I won't start using an AI answer box merely because a manager says the word modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep the Saturday appointment calls and repeat the date and travel instructions to each caller before ending the call. If this plateau continues into its first year, I'll work the same rota and keep our ordinary spending within our wages. I won't pay for a private AI service to do a job I can already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The clinic will still need appointments, and our wages look steady here. I would rather spend the extra minute making sure an older caller heard the right date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes wrong when a date is rushed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed visit turns into another call and sometimes another month waiting. A clinic caller's voice tells me when a missed appointment is more than a diary mistake. I ask the person to say the date back to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help if a bill went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would care, but their rent is their own burden. Ellis and I have the nine-month reserve for a real household surprise. I don't build a budget on the children coming over with an envelope.

say: I'd accept **routine reminders** while keeping a person on the appointment line.
I'd keep **dates and travel instructions** checked aloud with each caller.
think: I expect the **Saturday premium** and Ellis's bus shifts to continue.
I see our **nine-month reserve** as cover for real bills, not permission to buy new services.
do: Keep **Saturday clinic calls**; repeat dates and travel instructions, then ask patients to repeat dates.
Keep **ordinary household spending** within current paid wages while the rota holds.
feel: **Calm** about both wages, while still attentive to callers who may miss appointments.
S0.quote: A clinic caller's voice tells me when a missed appointment is more than a diary mistake.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI tools** and sees no reason to start in the mild picture.
Her **higher Saturday pay** and nine-month reserve support a steady mortgage budget.
Her careful **date readback** comes from missed-appointment experience, not a claim that all reminders fail.

steps.text: Keep Saturday clinic calls; repeat dates and travel instructions, then ask patients to repeat dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the system may book the easy changes, but somebody must be paid to put a mistake right. I would ask my manager for the Saturday rota in writing. I would not tell colleagues their hours are safe just because patients still need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the easy calls could disappear and take the premium with them. I don't pick up new systems quickly, and I have not used an AI tool. The nine-month reserve gives us time, but it does not recreate Saturday pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask my manager for the written Saturday rota and the rule for correcting an automated appointment. I'll keep handling paid changes and missed-visit calls while those shifts exist. I will not apply for a different job just for a title; if the written rota actually removes my paid Saturday hours, I'll look at posted local paid openings then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Losing the Saturday premium would change the mortgage sums, even if the weekday desk kept me. I can ask for a page of hours, but I cannot make the operator keep them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What correction authority would you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to move the appointment and tell the patient the new time, not just pass a complaint to another queue. A printed rota is the only answer I will trust about whether Saturday pay remains. The diary can be quick and still be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the written rota before applying elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have some savings, and there are other centres nearby, but they may use the same booking software. I would rather keep a paid Saturday than give it up for an unposted promise. If my premium actually goes, I will start checking paid roles.

say: I'd ask for a **written Saturday rota** and real appointment correction authority.
I'd say **patient help** still needs paid people when software makes a mistake.
think: I fear losing the **Saturday premium** before the whole job goes.
I know nearby centres may adopt the **same booking software**.
do: Ask the manager for the **written Saturday rota** and automated-appointment correction rule this year.
Keep **paid appointment calls** while shifts exist; look at posted paid roles only if Saturday hours are removed.
feel: **Anxious** that losing premium hours changes the mortgage calculation.
S1.quote: A printed rota is the only answer I will trust about whether Saturday pay remains.
fieldNote: Her **individual manager request** seeks a real rota and correction rule, not collective bargaining.
She explicitly **defers applications** until written paid Saturday hours are lost, despite several nearby centres.
Her concern is the **premium wage**, not an invented layoff in the mild transition.

steps.text: Keep paid clinic appointments and missed-visit calls while shifts exist
Defer other job applications until written Saturday rota removes paid hours
Check posted local paid roles only after written Saturday-hour loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ellis that full thinking AI by 2028 might answer appointment calls before the 2031 robots reach his buses. I would ask the clinic for an actual closure date. I would not claim that another reception desk is safe just because a person stands at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our call line and my higher Saturday pay to end quickly. Nine months saved protects the mortgage for a while, but my partner Ellis's bus wage cannot carry everything alone. His driving could face robots later, which makes a long gamble on reception even less attractive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll cancel the autumn city break and write down the mortgage, bus fares and weekly essentials with Ellis. If the clinic call line ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted paid walk-in hospital reception job only if the written weekly hours and wage after bus fare, together with Ellis's actual pay, cover our mortgage and essentials. I'll keep the paid clinic calls until the line ends and start a new job only after a written paid offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have time in the bank, but I expect to lose the week that fills it. I can ask for a real opening; I cannot make a hospital hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a walk-in reception desk if AI can book visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A patient who arrives confused still needs someone to show them the right corridor, though I know AI may shrink the desk as well. I would not leave a paid line for a rumour about a hospital job. I want the weekly hours and after-fare wage on paper before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ellis's bus work changes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would recalculate rather than assume his driving lasts forever. The 2031 robots are a later risk, not extra time for my calls. I won't ask our grown children to hold the mortgage.

say: I'd ask for the **clinic closure date** and written pay at any walk-in desk.
I'd tell Ellis **2028 AGI** reaches calls before 2031 robots reach buses.
think: I expect the **call line and premium** to end quickly.
I know nine months saved and Ellis's wage cannot cover the **mortgage indefinitely**.
do: Cancel the **autumn city break** and calculate mortgage, bus fares and weekly essentials with Ellis now.
After line closure, apply for **posted paid hospital reception** only if written weekly hours and after-bus household wages cover mortgage/essentials.
Keep **paid clinic calls** until line closure; start hospital work only after a written paid offer.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of the higher-paid week despite nine months saved.
S2.quote: Nine months saved protects the mortgage for a while, but my partner Ellis's bus wage cannot carry everything alone.
fieldNote: Her **hospital application** follows actual line closure and requires written weekly hours plus after-bus household coverage.
She keeps paid calls until closure and waits for a **written paid offer** before starting hospital work.
She recognises her partner's **bus work** faces a later robot risk, without treating reception as permanent safety.

steps.text: Cancel autumn city break and calculate mortgage bus fares and weekly essentials with Ellis
Check posted paid hospital reception’s written weekly hours and after-bus household wages against mortgage/essentials
Apply after clinic closure only if checked hospital terms cover mortgage and essentials
Keep paid clinic calls until closure; start hospital work only after written paid offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to find out whether the hospital still pays people to help walk-in patients, not just to print a certificate. The appointment line could still go in 2031. Robots around 2034 are a separate question for the hands-on parts of a hospital day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can stay on the clinic rota and build more of a buffer from the Saturday premium. I don't want to learn a new AI system for a job that may disappear with mine. I would rather see a real walk-in shift and its pay before spending our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll put part of each paid Saturday premium into our mortgage reserve and ask the hospital whether a posted paid walk-in shift can be observed on paid time. If it offers one, I'll watch how the desk helps people who arrive in person. In the first year after 2031, if the clinic cuts my paid hours, I'll apply for a still-posted paid walk-in job only if its written weekly hours and after-bus household wages cover mortgage and essentials; I'll keep any remaining paid clinic shifts until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me measure rather than bolt. I can learn a corridor by walking it; I cannot learn a wage from a poster. The hospital could decide it needs fewer receptionists too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch on that hospital shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the person at the desk can change a missed appointment or only point at a screen. I'd also count the bus trip home after the last shift. I would not train for a doorway that has no paid hours behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid walk-in opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my clinic wage if any hours remain and search the other posted local paid work against our mortgage budget. Ellis and I can use the reserve for a bounded search, not treat it as a second salary. I won't count a waiting list as a job.

say: I'd check for **posted paid walk-in hours** before changing jobs.
I'd say **2034 robots** may alter physical hospital tasks after 2031 AGI.
think: I can build the **mortgage reserve** while Saturday premiums still arrive.
I doubt an **AI course** or new title alone shields another desk.
do: Save **Saturday premium**; without a hospital opening, search other posted paid work against our mortgage budget using bounded reserve.
Ask to observe a **posted paid hospital shift** on paid time if offered; check appointment correction authority and last bus.
After 2031 paid-hour cuts, apply for **still-posted paid walk-in work** only if written after-bus household weekly wages/hours cover mortgage/essentials; sign before leaving.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test an actual paid shift and protect current wages.
S3.quote: I can learn a corridor by walking it; I cannot learn a wage from a poster.
fieldNote: She does **not adopt AI tools** merely because the timetable is longer; she inspects real patient-facing work.
The **paid observation** depends on a posted shift; the later application depends on actual clinic-hour cuts and written household coverage.
Remaining **clinic hours** continue until a written offer is signed; an unposted hospital waitlist is not income.

steps.text: Save part of each paid Saturday premium into mortgage reserve
Ask to observe posted paid hospital shift on paid time if offered; check correction authority/last-bus
Apply after 2031 cuts for still-posted paid walk-in if written after-bus household weekly wages/hours cover mortgage/essentials
Without hospital post, keep paid shifts until signed offer; search posted paid jobs within mortgage budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter a decade is a long time to check our own figures, but I won't declare us retired from an AI card. I would be sixty-eight in 2036. Some callers may still want a person even if the appointment software can do the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have nine months saved today and good Saturday pay, but ten years of mortgage and bills can eat through both. I don't know what retirement income we will actually have, if any. Ellis's bus work may change when physical robots arrive around 2039, so I won't promise his wage forever either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year Ellis and I will review our mortgage balance, savings and actual income every year, and I'll keep paid Saturday calls while they exist. I won't set a leaving date until documented resources cover years of essentials without my wage. If AGI ends the clinic line in the first year after 2036 and the budget still needs my pay, I'll apply for posted paid local walk-in work with written hours and after-bus household wages covering the mortgage and essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a quiet way. The decade gives us room to calculate, but no form can promise what our wages will be at sixty-eight. I would rather be cautious than ask our children to rescue a careless guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a leaving date believable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Statements showing continuing income and savings can cover the mortgage, food, travel and repairs for years, not a guessed benefit. A date on an AI card is not a statement from our bank. If the numbers are short, I keep a paid shift if one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to keep a room ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our children have their own keys; they are not our retirement plan. They can visit because they want to, not because I have pencilled their income into our budget. Ellis agrees about that.

say: I'd tell my daughter **ten years** permits real household sums, not an invented retirement date.
I'd say **2036 AGI** may end clinic calls even if I still need paid work.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** or Ellis's bus wage will cover bills indefinitely.
I may still need a **paid shift** at sixty-eight if verified household resources fall short.
do: Review **mortgage and income**, plus savings, with Ellis yearly while keeping paid Saturday calls.
Defer a **leaving date** until documented resources cover years of essentials without my wage.
After 2036 closure, seek **posted paid reception** if income remains short and written weekly hours/after-bus household pay cover mortgage/essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about future income despite having years to check and save.
S4.quote: A date on an AI card is not a statement from our bank.
fieldNote: She refuses to assume a **pension entitlement** or financial rescue from grown children.
Her **annual household review** gates any decision to stop paid work, with no fixed retirement date.
If 2036 calls close and money remains short, she seeks **posted paid work** on written after-bus household terms.

steps.text: Review mortgage savings and actual income with Ellis yearly; keep paid Saturday calls
Defer leaving work until documented resources cover years of essentials without clinic wages
Check posted paid reception’s written weekly hours and after-bus household pay against mortgage/essentials
Apply after 2036 clinic closure only if household income short and reception terms cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose the whole appointment line while the mortgage stays put. A true closure date, a posted paid hospital opening with weekly hours in writing, and a budget Ellis and I both understand would help. Our children have their own keys; they are not our retirement plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a person gets to a clinic after a changed appointment. The last bus isn't on the booking screen when somebody offers a late slot. I have heard that problem for years.

headlineQuote: Our children have their own keys; they are not our retirement plan.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Bianca handles clinic appointment calls carefully and has never used AI tools.
She has **secondary schooling**, higher Saturday-premium pay, about nine months saved, a mortgage and a partner who drives a bus.
She waits for **written hours loss** in slower change before checking other jobs.
Fast AGI pushes her toward **posted paid walk-in work** with household wage checks, while longer horizons prompt yearly budget reviews.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her whole appointment line and higher Saturday wage while the mortgage continues.
whatWouldHelp: A **real closure date**, posted paid hospital hours in writing and a shared household budget would help.
